    #sec[Introduction]
    #para[
      Quantifying ecosystem characteristics remains an important step toward data-driven conservation and restoration policy, and multiple data streams are available to this end. Data from capture-based surveys have been used alongside data from acoustic surveys for species identifiation "We used acoustic data and biological sampling information collected with two midwater trawl nets from a dedicated voyage, to train a classification tree algorithm" [1], but there is recent interest in non-lethal eDNA surveying as a species identification tool alongside acoustic surveying: previous work has 'allowed the observation of shifts in eDNA profiles concurrent with the movement of organisms in the DVM as measured by acoustic sensors'[2] and 'tested the utility of paired hydroacoustic and eDNA surveys by replicating samples over a 12-h period along the depth gradient of pelagic lake habitat where the fish community exhibits diel vertical migration' [3]. This study investigates eDNA, purse seine, acoustic and water quality data sets gathered in at three sites in July 2025 as potentially complementary information for inference of ecosystem characteristics.

      Quantifying baseline ecosystem characteristics remains an important step toward emergency (e.g., oil spill) preparedness and restoration efficacy. Multiple data types are available to this end. Previous work has shown (1)  [1–4] and (2)  [5–7]. Optimal data collection and analysis to create reliable inference is paramount when supporting decision making by tribal governments. This study investigates how four distinct data sources compare to one another, and how analysis of acoustic, eDNA, water quality and purse seine data in concert may lead to more comprehensive conclusions about baseline ecosytem characteristics.
